Cluster scattering coefficients in rank 22

Thomas Elgin , Nathan Reading and Salvatore Stella Thomas Elgin and Nathan ReadingDepartment of Mathematics, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA Email address, Nathan Reading (corresponding author) : reading@math.ncsu.edu Salvatore StellaDipartimento di Ingegneria e Scienze dell’Informazione e Matematica, Università degli Studi dell’Aquila, IT Email address, Salvatore Stella : salvatore.stella@univaq.it
Abstract.

We present conjectures on the scattering terms of cluster scattering diagrams of rank 22, supported by significant computational evidence.

1. Introduction

Scattering diagrams were introduced by Kontsevich, Soibelman, Gross, and Siebert in [14, 16] for the study of mirror symmetry. Cluster algebras were introduced by Fomin and Zelevinsky [7] for the study of total positivity, but quickly found algebraic, geometric, and combinatorial connections to a wide range of mathematical areas. Scattering diagrams became an essential tool in the structural study of cluster algebras when Gross, Hacking, Keel, and Kontsevich defined (and proved the existence of) cluster scattering diagrams [11]. Applying the scattering-diagram machinery of broken lines and theta functions that had been introduced and developed in various papers by Carl, Gross, Hacking, Keel, Pumperla, and Siebert [5, 9, 10, 12, 15], they corrected and proved a conjecture of Fock and Goncharov [6] on the cluster variety and several conjectures of Fomin and Zelevinsky on the structure of cluster algebras [8].

The defining data of a cluster scattering diagram is an exchange matrix, meaning a skew-symmetrizable integer matrix. Following the usual terminology in the cluster algebras literature, we will say that the cluster scattering diagram of an r×rr\times r exchange matrix is a cluster scattering diagram of “rank rr” (regardless of the rank of the matrix in the usual linear-algebraic sense).

A rank-rr scattering diagram lives in a real vector space of dimension rr and consists of walls (codimension-11 cones), each decorated by a scattering term (a multivariate formal power series). The cluster scattering diagram is defined by specifying that certain walls must be present and certain walls must not be present and then requiring a consistency condition. Some details of the definition, in rank 22, are given in Section 2. A rank-11 cluster scattering diagram is trivially easy to construct, but a typical rank-22 cluster scattering diagram is already extremely complicated, and completely explicit formulas are not known for coefficients of scattering terms. (This statement depends, of course, on what one calls “explicit”. See Section 4.)

Although cluster scattering diagrams of higher rank can be vastly more complicated, there is a sense in which cluster scattering diagrams of rank 22 tell much of the story about higher rank. The importance of rank 22 is seen in the proof of the existence of the cluster scattering diagram in general rank in [11, Appendix C]. That proof constructs the cluster scattering diagram degree by degree (in the sense of degrees of terms in the power series). To move the construction to the next degree, one adds higher order terms and new nontrivial walls to yield consistency up to that degree. The consistency is checked locally about every (n−2)(n-2)-dimensional intersection of walls (“joint”), and the local consistency condition is exactly the condition on a rank-22 cluster scattering diagram. Thus, in some sense, the construction of a general-rank cluster scattering diagram consists of constructing rank-22 cluster scattering diagrams all throughout the ambient space.

The purpose of this note is to record and share some conjectures on cluster scattering diagrams of rank 22 that are supported by significant computational evidence.

Remark. Since this note was posted on the arXiv, Ryota Akagi has made us aware that some of our conjectures can be proved using results from his paper [1]. Also, an anonymous referee pointed out some additional special cases of our conjectures that are known. Details on these connections are given in Section 4.

2. Cluster scattering diagrams of rank 22

We now give the definition of the cluster scattering diagram, specialized to rank 22 and following the notation of [17]. (See also [11, Example 1.15].) Up to symmetry, we may as well assume that the exchange matrix is B=[0c−b0]B=\begin{bmatrix}[r]0&\,c\\ -b&0\end{bmatrix} for b,c>0b,c>0.

Let NN be the lattice ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} with the usual basis {𝐞1,𝐞2}{\{\mathbf{e}_{1},\mathbf{e}_{2}\}} and let N∘N^{\circ} be the sublattice of NN generated by b​𝐞1b\hskip 0.7pt\mathbf{e}_{1} and c​𝐞2c\hskip 0.7pt\mathbf{e}_{2}. Let MM be the dual lattice to NN and let M∘M^{\circ} be the superlattice of MM that is dual to N∘N^{\circ}, with basis {𝐟1,𝐟2}{\{\mathbf{f}_{1},\mathbf{f}_{2}\}} such that ⟨𝐟1,b​𝐞1⟩=⟨𝐟2,c​𝐞2⟩=1{\langle\mathbf{f}_{1},b\hskip 0.7pt\mathbf{e}_{1}\rangle}={\langle\mathbf{f}_{2},c\hskip 0.7pt\mathbf{e}_{2}\rangle}=1 and ⟨𝐟1,𝐞2⟩=⟨𝐟2,𝐞1⟩=0{\langle\mathbf{f}_{1},\mathbf{e}_{2}\rangle}={\langle\mathbf{f}_{2},\mathbf{e}_{1}\rangle}=0. It is the interplay between NN and N∘N^{\circ}, and dually M∘M^{\circ} and MM, that integrates the skew-symmetrizability of BB seamlessly into the construction.

Take indeterminates z1z_{1} and z2z_{2} and define ζ1=z2c\zeta_{1}=z_{2}^{c} and ζ2=z1−b\zeta_{2}=z_{1}^{-b}. (In [11, Example 1.15], z1z_{1} and z2z_{2} are called A1A_{1} and A2A_{2}.) Given a vector n=n1​𝐞1+n2​𝐞2∈Nn=n_{1}\mathbf{e}_{1}+n_{2}\mathbf{e}_{2}\in N, we write ζn\zeta^{n} to mean ζ1n1​ζ2n2\zeta_{1}^{n_{1}}\zeta_{2}^{n_{2}}, and given m=m1​𝐟1+m2​𝐟2∈M∘m=m_{1}\mathbf{f}_{1}+m_{2}\mathbf{f}_{2}\in M^{\circ}, we write zmz^{m} to mean z1m1​z2m2z_{1}^{m_{1}}z_{2}^{m_{2}}.

A wall is a pair (𝔡,f𝔡)({\mathfrak{d}},f_{\mathfrak{d}}) where 𝔡{\mathfrak{d}} is a codimension-11 cone (thus a line through the origin or a ray with vertex at the origin) and f𝔡f_{\mathfrak{d}} is a formal power series in ζ1\zeta_{1} and ζ2\zeta_{2} satisfying the following conditions. The condition on 𝔡{\mathfrak{d}} is that there must exist a nonzero vector in NN with nonnegative entries that is normal to 𝔡{\mathfrak{d}}. Take nn to be such a vector that is primitive in NN. The condition on f𝔡f_{\mathfrak{d}} is that it has the form 1+∑ℓ≥1cℓ​ζℓ​n1+\sum_{\ell\geq 1}c_{\ell}\zeta^{\ell n}, or in other words f𝔡f_{\mathfrak{d}} is a univariate formal power series in ζn\zeta^{n} with constant term 11. The formal power series f𝔡f_{\mathfrak{d}} is called the scattering term on 𝔡{\mathfrak{d}}. A scattering diagram is a collection 𝔇{\mathfrak{D}} of walls, satisfying a finiteness condition that amounts to requiring that all of the relevant computations can be made by taking limits in the sense of formal power series. Specifically, the requirement is that for any k≥0k\geq 0, all but finitely many walls of 𝔇{\mathfrak{D}} are 11 plus terms with total degree >k>k in ζ1\zeta_{1} and ζ2\zeta_{2}.

This definition of a scattering diagram is so broad as to be almost meaningless; the condition that makes a scattering diagram interesting is consistency, which we now define. We begin by describing an action on formal Laurent series that is associated to crossing a wall. Given a wall 𝔡{\mathfrak{d}} having normal vector nn with nonnegative entries and given a path that crosses the wall transversely, the wall-crossing automorphism takes a Laurent monomial zmz^{m} to zm​f𝔡⟨m,±n′⟩z^{m}f_{\mathfrak{d}}^{{\langle m,\pm n^{\prime}\rangle}}, where n′n^{\prime} is the primitive vector in N∘N^{\circ} that is a positive scaling of nn. The sign in the formula is “−-” if the curve crosses in the direction that agrees with nn or “−-” if the curve crosses in the direction that disagrees with nn. We extend linearly and take limits to act on formal Laurent series. Using standard terminology, we call this a wall-crossing automorphism, but we need not be careful about the algebraic structure on which it acts as an automorphism. For us, it is just an action on formal Laurent series.

A path-ordered product is, loosely speaking, the composition of these wall-crossing automorphisms along a path. More correctly, since a path might intersect infinitely many walls, the path-ordered product is defined as a limit of formal Laurent series. For each k≥0k\geq 0, consider only those walls whose scattering terms have nontrivial terms of total degree ≤k\leq k. The finiteness condition on 𝔇{\mathfrak{D}} ensures that there are finitely many such walls, so we can compose the wall-crossing automorphism for those walls. The path-ordered product is the limit, in the sense of formal Laurent series, as k→∞k\to\infty. A scattering diagram is consistent if the path-ordered product for a small oriented circle about the origin is the identity map.

A wall with nonnegative normal n=n1​𝐞1+n2​𝐞2∈Nn=n_{1}\mathbf{e}_{1}+n_{2}\mathbf{e}_{2}\in N is outgoing if the vector −b​n2​𝐟1+c​n1​𝐟2∉𝔡-bn_{2}\mathbf{f}_{1}+cn_{1}\mathbf{f}_{2}\not\in{\mathfrak{d}}. One can check that, in any case, −b​n2​𝐟1+c​n1​𝐟2-bn_{2}\mathbf{f}_{1}+cn_{1}\mathbf{f}_{2} is in the line containing 𝔡{\mathfrak{d}}. Thus 𝔡{\mathfrak{d}} is outgoing if and only if it is a ray (rather than a line) and is contained in the fourth quadrant. The cluster scattering diagram is the unique consistent scattering diagram containing the walls (𝐞1⟂,1+z2c)(\mathbf{e}_{1}^{\perp},1+z_{2}^{c}) and (𝐞2⟂,1+z1−b)(\mathbf{e}_{2}^{\perp},1+z_{1}^{-b}) such that all other walls are outgoing.

For i,j≥0i,j\geq 0, define τ⁡(i,j)\tau(i,j) to be the coefficient of ζ1i​ζ2j=z1−j​b​z2i​c\zeta_{1}^{i}\zeta_{2}^{j}=z_{1}^{-jb}z_{2}^{ic} on the wall of the cluster scattering diagram that is orthogonal to i​𝐞1+j​𝐞2i\hskip 0.5pt\mathbf{e}_{1}+j\hskip 0.5pt\mathbf{e}_{2}. To specify or emphasize the exchange matrix, we may write τb,c​(i,j)\tau^{b,c}(i,j), but generally, we think of τ⁡(i,j)\tau(i,j) as a function of indeterminates bb and cc. We define g=gcd⁡(i​b,j​c)gcd⁡(i,j)g=\frac{\gcd(ib,jc)}{\gcd(i,j)}.

Remark on symmetry. We point out the obvious symmetry τb,c​(i,j)=τc,b​(j,i)\tau^{b,c}(i,j)=\tau^{c,b}(j,i). Another symmetry is less obvious but not hard to prove using mutation of scattering diagrams: Interpreting (i,j)(i,j) as a vector i​𝐞1+j​𝐞2i\hskip 0.5pt\mathbf{e}_{1}+j\hskip 0.5pt\mathbf{e}_{2} in the root lattice of a root system with Cartan matrix [2−c−b2]\begin{bmatrix}[r]2&-c\\ -b&2\end{bmatrix} and simple roots 𝐞1\mathbf{e}_{1} and 𝐞2\mathbf{e}_{2}, the integers τb,c​(i,j)\tau^{b,c}(i,j) are invariant under the action of the Weyl group on (i,j)(i,j). This amounts to the symmetries τb,c​(i,j)=τb,c​(i,−j+c​i)\tau^{b,c}(i,j)=\tau^{b,c}(i,-j+ci) and τb,c​(i,j)=τb,c​(−i+b​j,j)\tau^{b,c}(i,j)=\tau^{b,c}(-i+bj,j).

3. Conjectures on coefficients of scattering terms

Conjectures.

  1.   1.

    For i,j>0i,j>0, the coefficient τ⁡(i,j)\tau(i,j) is a polynomial in bb, cc, and gg.

  2.   2.

    The polynomial has gg as a factor and its degree in gg is gcd⁡(i,j)\gcd(i,j).

  3.   3.

    Its degree in bb is j−1j-1 and its degree in cc is i−1i-1.

  4.   4.

    The polynomial (max⁡(i,j))!​τ​(i,j)(\max(i,j))!\,\,\tau(i,j) has integer coefficients.

  5.   5.

    τ⁡(1,j)=gb​(bj)\displaystyle\tau(1,j)=\frac{g}{b}\binom{b}{j}

  6.   6.

    τ⁡(i,1)=gc​(ci)\displaystyle\tau(i,1)=\frac{g}{c}\binom{c}{i}

  7.   7.

    τ⁡(i,i)=g(b−1)​(c−1)​i+g​((b−1)​(c−1)​i+gi)\displaystyle\tau(i,i)=\frac{g}{(b-1)(c-1)i+g}\binom{(b-1)(c-1)i+g}{i}

  8.   8.

    τ⁡(i,i)=∑ℓ=0∞gℓ+1​(i−1ℓ)​(i⁡(b​c−b−c)+g−1ℓ)\displaystyle\tau(i,i)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\frac{g}{\ell+1}\binom{i-1}{\ell}\binom{i(bc-b-c)+g-1}{\ell}

  9.   9.

    τ⁡(i,i−1)=gi⁡(i​b−i+1)​((i​b−i+1)​(c−1)i−1)\displaystyle\tau(i,i-1)=\frac{g}{i(ib-i+1)}\binom{(ib-i+1)(c-1)}{i-1}

  10.   10.

    τ⁡(j−1,j)=gj⁡(j​c−j+1)​((j​c−j+1)​(b−1)j−1)\displaystyle\tau(j-1,j)=\frac{g}{j(jc-j+1)}\binom{(jc-j+1)(b-1)}{j-1}

  11.   11.

    τb,b​(i,j)\tau^{b,b}(i,j) is a polynomial in bb of degree i+j−1i+j-1 that expands positively in the basis {(b0),(b1),(b2),…}{\{\binom{b}{0},\binom{b}{1},\binom{b}{2},\ldots\}}.

  12.   12.

    τb,b​(i,j)\tau^{b,b}(i,j) has unimodal log-concave coefficients.

  13.   13.

    τ1,5​(2​j,j)=1j​∑ℓ=0∞(ℓj−ℓ+1)​(j+ℓ−1ℓ)\displaystyle\tau^{1,5}(2j,j)=\frac{1}{j}\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\binom{\ell}{j-\ell+1}\binom{j+\ell-1}{\ell}.

Comments.

  • •

    Conjectures 5 and 6 are symmetric and Conjectures 9 and 10 are symmetric.

  • •

    Conjecture 8 is equivalent to Conjecture 7.

  • •

    Since c=bc=b in Conjectures 11 and 12, also g=bg=b.

Assuming Conjecture 1, write τ⁡(i,j,k)\tau(i,j\,;k) for the coefficient of gkg^{k} in τ⁡(i,j)\tau(i,j) and similarly τb,c​(i,j,k)\tau^{b,c}(i,j\,;k). Because gg is also invariant under the action of the Weyl group on (i,j)(i,j), we have τb,c​(i,j,k)=τb,c​(i,−j+b​i,k)\tau^{b,c}(i,j;k)=\tau^{b,c}(i,-j+bi;k) and τb,c​(i,j,k)=τb,c​(−i+a​j,j,k)\tau^{b,c}(i,j;k)=\tau^{b,c}(-i+aj,j;k).

Conjectures.

  1.   14.

    τ⁡(i,j,k)\tau(i,j\,;k) is a polynomial of degree j−kj-k in bb and degree i−ki-k in cc and has a term that is a nonzero constant times bj−k​ci−kb^{j-k}c^{i-k}.

  2.   15.

    If gcd⁡(i,j)=1\gcd(i,j)=1, then τ⁡(i​k,j​k,k)=τ​(i,j,1)kk!\displaystyle\tau(ik,jk\,;k)=\frac{\tau(i,j\,;1)^{k}}{k!}.

  3.   16.

    τ⁡(k,j​k,k−1)=τ​(1,j,1)k−1⋅pj(k−2)!\displaystyle\tau(k,jk\,;k-1)=\frac{\tau(1,j\,;1)^{k-1}\cdot p_{j}}{(k-2)!}, where pjp_{j} is a polynomial in bb and cc that depends only on jj, not kk.

  4.   17.

    τ⁡(i​k,k,k−1)=τ​(i,1,1)k−1⋅pi(k−2)!\displaystyle\tau(ik,k\,;k-1)=\frac{\tau(i,1\,;1)^{k-1}\cdot p_{i}}{(k-2)!}, where pip_{i} is a polynomial in bb and cc that depends only on ii, not kk.

  5.   18.

    If gcd⁡(i,j)=1\gcd(i,j)=1, then τ⁡(k​i,k​j,k−1)\tau(ki,kj\,;k-1) has a factor pi​jp_{ij} that depends only on ii and jj, not on kk, and the other factors of τ⁡(k​i,k​j,k−1)\tau(ki,kj\,;k-1) also appear as factors of τ⁡(i,j,1)\tau(i,j\,;1).

Remark on computation. These conjectures are backed up by significant computational evidence. The functions τ⁡(i,j)\tau(i,j) of bb and cc can be computed symbolically up to large values of ii and jj. Thus, for example, the polynomials shown in the first example in Section 2 are known to be correct for all bb and cc, rather than only for some specific values of bb and cc. Similarly, the conjectures on τ⁡(i,j)\tau(i,j) in this section have been checked for many values of ii and jj, and each case that has been checked is true for all bb and cc.

Computing the functions τ⁡(i,j)\tau(i,j) proceeds by induction on i+ji+j, by solving, at each step, the equations that describe consistency of the cluster scattering diagram in degree i+ji+j using known values of τ⁡(i′,j′)\tau(i^{\prime},j^{\prime}) for i′+j′<i+ji^{\prime}+j^{\prime}<i+j. Thus, it would be significant progress even to find a recursive description of τ⁡(i,j)\tau(i,j) whose recursive step is simpler than solving a system of equations.

The code we used in our experiments together with precomputed data up to degree 20 is available at https://github.com/Etn40ff/scatcoef/.

4. Related work

Work of Ryota Akagi [1] also aims at explicitly understanding scattering terms in the cluster scattering diagram, but with different approach and conventions. His work is independent of ours, was posted before we publicized any of our conjectures, and also contains results in different directions that we did not conjecture. Akagi has informed us of a forthcoming paper [2] in which he proves Conjectures 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, and 15, as well as part of Conjecture 14 and a result that is similar to Conjectures 16, 17, and 18, using his results from [1].

Tom Bridgeland [3, Theorem 1.5] identifies the cluster scattering diagram with the stability scattering diagram in the case b=cb=c, thus realizing τb,b​(i,j)\tau^{b,b}(i,j) as the Euler characteristic of a certain moduli scheme of representations of the associated Jacobi algebra.

An anonymous referee pointed out that Conjectures 7 and 9 (and symmetrically 10) generalize results of Reineke and Weist [19]. Specifically, the case g=1g=1 of Conjecture 7 is [19, Corollary 11.2] (which proves a conjecture of Gross and Pandharipande [13, Conjecture 1.4]) and the case g=1g=1 of Conjecture 9 is [19, Theorem 9.4]. In comparing Conjecture 7 with [19, Corollary 11.2], it is useful to notice that after setting g=1g=1, the right side of Conjecture 7 can be rewritten as 1(b​c−b−c)​i+1​((b−1)​(c−1)​ii)\frac{1}{(bc-b-c)i+1}\binom{(b-1)(c-1)i}{i}.

Gross, Hacking, Keel, and Kontsevich [11, Example 1.15] state the case b=cb=c of Conjecture 8 and attribute its proof to Reineke [18].

Burcroff, Lee, and Mou have recently given a formula for the coefficients of scattering terms as a weighted sum over certain combinatorial objects called tight gradings [4, Theorem 1.1]. They intend to explore some of the conjectures of this paper using tight gradings [4, Section 9.2]. It would also be interesting to understand how the Weyl group symmetry appears in the combinatorics of tight gradings. (See the remark on symmetry at the end of Section 2.)
